builder_plan.scenario: You already need task-specific training and want to reduce its memory or compute cost.
builder_plan.change: Change only the training technique on a small controlled run after checking prerequisites.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current training recipe with the same model, data split, and evaluation.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Held-out quality, peak memory, training time, and full compute cost to the target quality.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Massive Activations Confound Sparse Autoencoders
summary: The method replaces training a sparse autoencoder on raw model activations with training on activations whose first principal component (massive-activation direction) has been removed, then adding PC1 back to the reconstruction. The cost is a PCA computation over collected activations, a modified training pipeline, and separate handling of the PC1 component, with negligible inference-time impact since SAEs are analysis artifacts. It can fail on models without dominant massive activations (where PC1 removal is unnecessary), if the PCA basis is computed on an unrepresentative activation sample, or if downstream interpretation requires features that partially load on PC1.
rationale: For a small team using SAEs to interpret frozen models, this is a cheap, well-specified correction to a demonstrated failure mode, but its benefit depends on whether the target model actually exhibits massive activations and requires validating feature-stability gains on the team's own checkpoints.

claims.statement: The method replaces training a sparse autoencoder on raw model activations with training on activations whose first principal component (massive-activation direction) has been removed, then adding PC1 back to the reconstruction. The cost is a PCA computation over collected activations, a modified training pipeline, and separate handling of the PC1 component, with negligible inference-time impact since SAEs are analysis artifacts. It can fail on models without dominant massive activations (where PC1 removal is unnecessary), if the PCA basis is computed on an unrepresentative activation sample, or if downstream interpretation requires features that partially load on PC1.

At the same TopK sparsity, the resulting SAE degrades the model up to 44% less and reduces content reconstruction error by up to 33.9%; top-50 feature sharing across runs rises from 4-39.5% to 73-99.5%.
